summary: This unit teaches you to give sound policy advice to a board, a permanent secretary or a chief executive in a public body: define the problem, gather and weigh evidence, choose policy instruments, appraise options with simple cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness sums, check equity, legal power, risk and unintended effects, and write a clear recommendation. You will also learn to evaluate an existing policy and to advise on national policy. It is written for officers and managers in Jamaican ministries, agencies and municipal corporations.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you to **advise on organisation policy**: to help the people who decide (a board, a minister, a permanent secretary, a chief executive officer or a municipal corporation's council) to make a good choice, and then to help them check that the choice worked.

A **policy** is a settled course of action that an organisation adopts to deal with an issue or reach an aim. A **public policy** is made by a government body and affects citizens, businesses or staff. Examples in Jamaica: how a municipal corporation licenses street vendors, how an agency collects overdue fees, how a ministry gives school-feeding support, how a public body protects the personal data of its clients.

The **policy adviser** does not decide. The adviser analyses the issue, gathers evidence, sets out realistic options with their costs, benefits and risks, recommends one, and explains why. The decision belongs to the person or body with authority. Advice must be honest, balanced, timely and clear, and you must be able to show where every fact came from.

**Who it is for:** supervisors, officers and managers in ministries, departments, agencies and municipal corporations who are asked to prepare policy papers, briefs or recommendations, and trainees who want to show that they can do so at Level 5.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Define the policy problem
Say what the problem is, how big it is, who is affected and why it happens, using a problem tree and the figures available.
Gather and weigh evidence
Use records, surveys, research and the experience of others, judge how reliable each source is, and avoid false conclusions about cause and effect.
Set policy objectives
Write objectives that say what will change, by how much and by when, so options can be judged against them.
Identify and choose policy instruments
Know the main tools (regulation, incentives, information, direct provision, partnership) and match them to the cause of the problem.
Appraise options
Compare at least three options, including keeping the present policy, using cost-benefit, cost-effectiveness and weighted scoring, and work every sum twice.
Check equity, feasibility, law, risk and side effects
Ask who gains or loses, whether the body can deliver, whether it has legal power, what could go wrong and what nobody planned.
Write and present advice
Produce a short, well-ordered paper with a clear recommendation, honest evidence, correct figures and a plan to monitor results.
Evaluate an existing policy and advise on national policy
Judge a running policy for relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, equity and sustainability, and explain a national policy to your own board.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions on problems, evidence, instruments, appraisal sums, equity, advice writing and evaluation.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as policy instruments, counterfactual, equity) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practical tasks**: analyse a problem and appraise options from an issue pack, and evaluate an existing policy and brief the board. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, by two different routes. A policy paper with a wrong figure loses the board's trust in the whole paper.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Policy, the policy cycle and the adviser's role

blocks.p: Public policy is made in stages that repeat. The usual model is the **policy cycle**. Knowing where a request sits in the cycle tells you what kind of advice is wanted.

flow: Agenda setting: the issue is recognised as one that needs action
Formulation: options are developed and appraised
Decision: the person or body with authority chooses
Implementation: the policy is put into effect
Evaluation: results are checked and the policy is kept, changed or ended

blocks.p: The adviser is most active at **formulation** (building and appraising options) and **evaluation** (judging what has happened), but also helps at agenda setting (spotting emerging problems) and implementation (advising on delivery problems).

blocks.h: Green Papers and White Papers in Jamaica

blocks.p: For major national policies the Government of Jamaica usually follows a consultation process. A **Green Paper** sets out proposals and options for **public discussion**; it invites views and is not yet the settled position. After consultation, a **White Paper** sets out the **approved policy**, often with the changes made because of what people said. Some policies then need new laws, which go to Parliament. Each ministry has a policy unit that coordinates this work.

head: Document
What it does
Status
rows: Green Paper
Sets out the problem, options and proposals; asks the public and stakeholders for comment
Proposal for discussion; nothing is decided
White Paper
States the policy the Government has adopted and how it will be put into effect
Approved policy
Cabinet submission or board paper
Asks the decision-maker to approve a policy, with advice and a recommendation
Advice for decision

blocks.h: What a good adviser does and does not do

head: The adviser does
The adviser does not
rows: Analyse the issue and give sound options and advice
Make the final policy decision for the body
Give honest, complete advice, including unwelcome evidence
Leave out evidence because the decision-maker prefers another answer
Recommend one option and give reasons
Hand over a list of options with no view
Accept the decision and help to carry it out well
Quietly undermine a decision that went against the advice
Keep confidential material confidential
Brief the media or outside parties unless authorised

blocks.note: If a senior colleague tells you to leave out evidence that does not support a preferred option, include it and raise your concern through the proper channel. Honest advice protects the body, the decision-maker and you.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Know the **legal and policy setting** before you advise: the body's own law or mandate, the government's stated priorities, national policies that bind all public bodies, and the rules on procurement, data protection and public finance. Advice that ignores them can lead the body into an unlawful or unaffordable position.

sections.title: Defining the problem and setting objectives

blocks.p: A request such as 'complaints about the agency are rising' is a **symptom**, not a defined problem. If you jump to a solution (a new policy, more staff) you may fix the wrong thing. First define the problem.

ul: **What** is happening? Describe it in facts (for example, 'late renewals').
**How big** is it? Use numbers and trends over several years, not impressions.
**Who** is affected? Identify the **target group**: the people the policy is meant to help or influence, such as tenants in arrears, small vendors or rural households.
**Why** is it happening? Look for causes, not only effects.

blocks.p: A **problem tree** is a diagram that puts the core problem in the trunk, the **causes** in the roots below it, and the **effects** in the branches above it. It stops you mixing up causes and effects, and it shows where a policy could act.

head: Part of the tree
What goes there
Example: late payment of market-stall fees
rows: Branches (effects)
What follows from the problem
Less money for market repairs; unfair to those who pay; complaints about a dirty market
Trunk (core problem)
The problem in one short statement
Many stallholders pay their fees months late
Roots (causes)
Why the problem happens
Some do not know the due date; only one payment office with short hours; no follow-up when fees are late

blocks.p: Policy should act on **causes**. A campaign to shame late payers treats an effect; adding payment points and reminders treats causes.

A **policy objective** states what the policy is meant to achieve. Options are judged against it. Make it **SMART**: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Give a **baseline** (where you are now) and a **target** (where you want to be).

head: Weak objective
SMART objective
rows: Improve payment of fees
Cut arrears on stall fees from J$18 million to below J$9 million by 31 March
Make licensing faster
Decide 90% of licence applications within 15 working days by December
Help more young people find jobs
Place 1,000 trainees in work within six months of completing training by the end of the financial year

blocks.note: An objective that says 'improve' or 'strengthen' with no number or date cannot be measured and so cannot be evaluated. Before a policy starts, agree how success will be measured.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **logic model** shows how a policy is expected to work: **inputs** (money, staff) lead to **activities** (training sessions), which produce **outputs** (people trained), which lead to **outcomes** (people in jobs) and eventually to **impact** (lower youth unemployment). Each arrow rests on an **assumption**, such as 'employers need the skills being taught'. The adviser tests the assumptions. If the assumption is wrong, the policy will fail even if it is carried out perfectly.

Policy also needs to **fit with other policies**. **Policy coherence** means that policies of different units, ministries and levels work together. Map the policies on the issue, then look for **gaps** (an important issue with no policy) and **overlaps or conflicts** (two policies with different rules on the same matter). Advise aligning conflicting policies and filling the gaps, and seek a joined-up approach with other ministries.

sections.title: Evidence: finding it, weighing it and using it

blocks.p: **Evidence-based advice** rests on sound data, research and analysis, not on opinion or on whoever speaks loudest. You must also show the reader how reliable the evidence is.

head: Source
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Administrative records (the body's own files, complaints, licences issued)
Cheap, covers everything the body handles
May be out of date or incomplete; records only people who came forward
National statistics (for example the Statistical Institute of Jamaica, labour force surveys)
Trends and comparisons across the island
Too broad for one parish; published with a delay
Sample surveys
What people know, do and want
Biased if the sample is not fair, for example only people who can be reached by phone
Consultation responses (Green Paper submissions, focus groups)
Views and reasons; spots problems you had not thought of
Organised groups may be louder than ordinary citizens; counting responses is not a vote
Research and evaluations of earlier programmes
What worked elsewhere and why
Local conditions may differ
Staff and stakeholder experience
Practical knowledge of delivery
Personal views; check against data

blocks.p: **Benchmarking** means studying how other countries, agencies or parishes handled a similar issue. It shows what has worked and what to avoid, but you must check whether it **suits local conditions**: an idea that works in a city with strong broadband may not work in a rural parish.

ul: **Fair and relevant**: does the sample represent the people affected? A fair sample survey of parents, plus route data, is stronger evidence on school transport than a few strong complaints.
**Current**: how old is it?
**Source**: who collected it and why? Does it have an interest in the answer?
**Consistent**: do other sources agree? If two studies disagree, report both, explain the difference and say which you weigh more and why.

blocks.p: Be careful with claims that a policy 'caused' a change. Crime fell 10% after street lights were put up in a town: did the lights cause it? Check whether crime also fell in **similar towns without new lights**. The **counterfactual** is the comparison case that shows what would have happened without the policy. Compare the covered group with a similar group not covered, or with the same group before and after, and ask what else changed (extra staff, a new law, the weather).

head: Result reported
Question to ask
rows: A pilot cut waiting times by 40% in one office
Did that office have extra staff or other help during the pilot? If so, the result may be overstated
Arrears fell after a letter campaign
Did arrears fall in places with no campaign? Was there a new penalty at the same time?
Attendance rose at schools with a feeding programme
Were those schools different in the first place (for example, already improving)?

ul: **Percentage** = part divided by whole, times 100. A survey of 600 businesses where 420 support a proposal: 420 / 600 = 0.70, so **70%**.
**Percentage change** = (new - old) divided by old, times 100.
**Percentage points** are the difference between two percentages: from 48% to 62% is a rise of 14 percentage points, not 14%.
**Date counting**: advice due 7 days before a board meeting on 28 March must be sent by **21 March**.

blocks.note: Where the evidence is thin, say so. State your assumptions (for example, 'take-up of 60%') so the reader can judge how reliable the forecast is. Do not hide uncertainty to look confident.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Policy instruments: the tools of policy

blocks.p: **Policy instruments** (also called policy tools) are the means a public body uses to achieve a policy aim. Choose the instrument that fits the **cause** of the problem. A single instrument is rarely enough, so advisers often recommend a **mix**.

head: Instrument
How it works
Example
Strength
Weakness
rows: Regulation
Requires or forbids behaviour by law; licences, standards, bans
A licence for food vendors; a ban on a type of plastic
Clear and strong where compliance is monitored
Costly to enforce; can burden small firms
Financial incentives (and disincentives)
Changes the cost or reward of a choice: grants, subsidies, fee discounts, fines, taxes
A fee discount for households that sort waste
Flexible; people choose
Costs money; may reward people who would have acted anyway
Information and education
Gives people facts and persuades them to change
A public campaign on safe food handling
Cheap, builds understanding
Slow; may not change behaviour alone
Direct provision
The body supplies the service itself
A municipal corporation runs a market
Control over quality and access
Needs budget and staff
Partnership and contracting
Work with private firms, NGOs or communities
A community group runs a recycling depot
Shares cost and skill
Needs oversight; risk of poor delivery

blocks.h: Matching the instrument to the cause

head: Evidence shows...
Most suitable first response
rows: Most small vendors break a hygiene rule because they do not know it exists
Inform and train vendors, then enforce against those who still break it (proportionate)
Most late renewals happen because people never receive the reminder letter
Add text and email reminders to letters
People know the rule but find compliance too costly
Incentive, grant or phased support
A small group knowingly breaks the rule for profit
Enforcement and penalties under the regulation

blocks.p: **Proportionality** means the response should fit the size and cause of the problem. Jumping straight to heavy enforcement when people simply have not been told is unfair and may be wasteful. A common sequence is **inform, support, then enforce**.

An options paper should include **keeping the current policy** (sometimes called the 'do nothing' or 'status quo' option). It is the standard against which all other options are judged. It shows decision-makers what happens if they do not change anything, and sometimes it turns out to be the best choice.

Give decision-makers a **real choice**. Options such as 'raise fees', 'make savings in services', 'find new revenue' or a mix are different. Three versions of the same idea are not different options. Where a parish municipal corporation must close a J$40 million funding gap, a real set of options might be fee rises, service savings, new revenue sources or a mix of them.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, a municipal corporation can only use powers its law gives it. Before advising a new fee or by-law, confirm that the body has the legal power to do it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Appraising options: costs, benefits and scoring

blocks.p: **Option appraisal** compares the options against the objective, using the same criteria for each. The tools below are simple, but you must apply them correctly and **work every sum twice**.
**Cost-benefit analysis (CBA)** puts a money value on both costs and benefits. Two measures are common.

head: Measure
Formula
Example: cost J$20 m, benefits J$36 m
rows: Net benefit
Benefits minus costs
Benefit-cost ratio (BCR)
Benefits divided by costs

blocks.p: A BCR above 1 means benefits exceed costs. **Net benefit** shows the size of the gain; the **ratio** shows the return per J$1 spent. They can point to different options, so look at both.

head: Option
Cost
Benefit
Net benefit
BCR
rows: A
J$40 m
J$60 m
J$20 m
B
J$25 m
J$35 m
J$10 m
C
J$20 m
J$36 m
J$16 m
D
J$50 m
J$80 m
J$30 m

blocks.p: Here D has the highest net benefit (J$30 m) but C has the highest ratio (1.8). If money is limited, the ratio helps you choose the best return; if the budget is enough, the net benefit may matter more. State which and why.

When costs and savings fall in different years, set them out year by year. **Simple payback** = cost divided by yearly saving. A system costing J$15 million and saving J$3 million a year pays back in 15 / 3 = **5 years**. If savings start only in year 2, add one year to the wait. Use the cumulative total: cost J$12 m in year 1, savings J$4 m a year from year 2: totals are 4 (end of year 2), 8 (year 3), 12 (year 4), so payback is by **the end of year 4**.

Remember **whole-life costs**: a registry choosing between more staff (J$30 m a year for five years = J$150 m) and a system (J$45 m once plus J$5 m a year for five years = 45 + 25 = J$70 m) must compare totals over the same period.

When benefits are hard to value in money, use **cost-effectiveness**: cost per unit of result. Programme X costs J$18 m and places 1,200 young people in jobs: 18,000,000 / 1,200 = **J$15,000 per job**. Programme Y costs J$15 m and places 750: 15,000,000 / 750 = **J$20,000 per job**. X is more cost-effective. Always say what the 'unit' is (per job, per household, per day of waiting removed).

**Weighted scoring** (a multi-criteria method) gives each criterion a **weight** according to its importance and each option a **score** against each criterion. Multiply score by weight and add up. With cost weighted 60% and impact 40%, an option scoring 5 for cost and 9 for impact gets 0.6 x 5 + 0.4 x 9 = 3.0 + 3.6 = **6.6**. Agree the weights before scoring to avoid fitting them to a favourite option, and show them to the reader.
Suitable general criteria for comparing options: **cost, benefit, risk, fairness (equity) and ease of delivery**.

blocks.h: Finance sums for fees and revenue

ul: **Net revenue** = (fee x number of payers) - cost of collecting it. A J$1,500 fee on 8,000 permits raises J$12,000,000; less J$2,000,000 to collect = **J$10,000,000**.
**Allow for behaviour change.** If a new fee is expected to cut applications by 10%, use 8,000 x 0.9 = **7,200** permits in the estimate.
**Regulatory cost** = number of firms x hours x value of an hour. 2,500 firms x 6 hours x J$1,200 = **J$18,000,000** a year.

blocks.note: Do not count a figure twice, mix years or forget the cost of collection. State the period and the assumptions beside every sum.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Equity, feasibility, law, risk and unintended effects

blocks.p: A policy that looks good in the sums can still fail the board's wider tests. A complete paper checks the following for **every** option.

head: Check
Question the adviser asks
Example
rows: Equity
Who gains and who loses? Are rural, poor, elderly, disabled or small-business groups treated fairly?
An online-only service saves money but may shut out rural elderly people; advise keeping an assisted option
Feasibility
Can the body deliver it: staff, skills, systems, time and money?
An option needs trained staff the agency does not have; the advice must include training time and cost
Legal power
Does the body have power to do this? Does it comply with other laws?
A new fee needs legal authority; sharing client records with a partner must follow the data protection law
Risk
What could go wrong, how likely and how serious, and how would it be managed?
Low take-up; cost overrun; delay in IT
Unintended consequences
What could this cause that nobody planned, good or bad?
Raising town-centre parking fees to cut traffic may push drivers onto nearby residential streets
Coherence
Does it fit with, or conflict with, other policies?
Closing small rural health posts conflicts with a plan to extend rural services

blocks.p: **Equity** is the fairness of how a policy's costs and benefits fall on different groups. It is not the same as treating everyone identically: a service that looks equal on paper may be unequal in practice if some people cannot reach it. Set out the gainers and losers, and suggest ways to reduce harm (assisted service, phased start, exemptions for the poorest).

A municipal corporation considers banning vending on the main street of a busy town. Possible unintended effects: vendors lose income and move to side streets or unsafe spots; customers go elsewhere; the town centre loses life; vendors may refuse to pay fees later. Good advice names them, estimates which are likely, and suggests ways to manage them: a relocation market in a good location, consultation with vendors, a phased start and monitoring.

Where evidence is mixed and the cost of error is high, recommend a **pilot** (a small-scale trial in one area) with evaluation before wider roll-out. A good pilot has a clear question, a fair comparison, a set period, agreed measures and a decision date. Show **sensitivity analysis**: results under different assumptions. For example, if take-up could be 40% or 70%, show both and what changes between them.

A **regulatory impact assessment (RIA)** weighs the costs and benefits of a proposed rule for those affected. It asks: is a rule needed? Are there lighter alternatives? What will it cost businesses (for example 2,500 small firms spending 6 hours a year on paperwork)? Are small firms treated proportionately? It usually includes consultation with those affected.

blocks.note: When advice touches personal information about citizens, check the body's duties under the data protection law (the purpose of the law is to protect personal data and limit its use). Use only the data needed and remove names where possible.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Coordinating input:** ask finance, legal, human resources and technical units to test the costs, legal risks and delivery points before you finalise. Consult affected agencies and reflect their views when advice affects them.
Busy decision-makers read the first page. Put what they need there.

blocks.h: Structure of a short policy paper

flow: Issue and recommendation (executive summary): the problem, what you recommend and the main reasons
Background and problem analysis: causes, size, target group
Options: at least three, including keeping the present policy, each with costs, benefits and risks
Appraisal: how options compare against the criteria, with correct figures
Implications: financial, legal, staffing, equity and risk effects
Recommendation, next steps and how results will be monitored
Sources and data in an annex so evidence can be checked

blocks.p: In a **short brief** (for example one page for a minister who has two minutes to read before a press conference), lead with the key facts, the recommendation and any lines to take. In a **longer paper**, keep an executive summary first and put detail in annexes.

ul: **Recommend one option** with reasons from the analysis. If the chair asks for your view, give it.
**Use plain language** and explain technical terms. Adapt content and format to each audience: the board, community leaders and front-line staff need different versions.
**List sources and data** so the evidence can be checked and trusted.
**Meet the deadline.** If papers must reach the board secretary 7 days before the meeting, work back from that date. If the full analysis is not ready, give interim advice and state its limits.
**Correct errors quickly.** If you find a wrong figure after sending, tell the decision-maker promptly and send a correction.
**Be honest about the unknown.** Say what you do not know and how you would find out.

blocks.p: A paper normally covers **financial, legal, staffing, equity and risk** implications. Add technology, communication and environmental effects where relevant.

When a new national policy binds all public bodies (for example, to publish service standards or to reduce paper use), advise your board **first** on what it requires, where the body stands against it (the gaps), what it will cost and how to comply, with a timetable and owners.

ul: If the decision differs from your advice, **accept it and help to carry it out well**. Record your advice and the evidence.
Recommend **how and when results will be checked** whenever you recommend adopting a policy.
Keep **records** of advice: what was advised, when and on what evidence.

blocks.note: Integrity rules: never suppress evidence, never accept gifts from parties affected by your advice, declare any conflict of interest, and do not share draft advice with outside parties.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Advisers are also asked: should this policy continue, change or end? **Policy evaluation** judges a running policy against the aims it was set to achieve. Use clear criteria.

head: Criterion
Question
Example evidence
rows: Relevance
Does it still address a real and current need?
Is the problem still there? Has a national policy or the context changed?
Effectiveness
Has it achieved its intended outcomes?
Results compared with the baseline and with a comparison group
Efficiency
Could the results be had at lower cost?
Cost per person helped; comparison with other ways of doing it
Equity
Who benefits and who is missed?
Results by area, income, age, gender, disability
Sustainability
Will the results last if funding or staff change?
Dependence on one-off or donor funding; local ownership

blocks.p: A parish homework-support policy covered schools where the pass rate rose from 48% to 62%. In similar schools without it, the rate rose from 48% to 55%. The **comparison group** shows that part of the rise would have happened anyway. The best estimate of the policy's effect is 14 - 7 = **7 percentage points**. If it cost J$24 million a year for 960 students, the cost per student is 24,000,000 / 960 = **J$25,000**.

flow: Confirm the policy's aims and logic model
Collect results, costs, survey findings and complaints
Compare with the baseline and with a similar group not covered
Judge each criterion with evidence, not opinion
Check equity, legal and staffing implications
Recommend continue, change or end, with implications and a review date

blocks.p: A good evaluation also asks whether the policy had **unintended results**, how it fits with national policy, and what lessons apply elsewhere. Report findings impartially, including those that disappoint.

blocks.note: Keep what is evaluated (the policy) separate from who delivered it (people). Evaluate against agreed aims, not against what you think the aims should have been.
blocks.label: Tip

c1.title: Stall fees at the Mandeville market
c1.text: The Manchester Municipal Corporation is owed J$18 million in stall fees by vendors at the Mandeville market. A survey of 150 of the 400 stallholders found that 90 did not know the date fees fall due. Fees can be paid at one office, open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. on weekdays, and the market trades mostly early on Saturdays and Sundays. Arrears are not followed up for months. The finance committee asks the policy officer, Marcia Reid, for advice.

c2.title: Water tanks for rural households in St Elizabeth
c2.text: A ministry is choosing how to help rural households in St Elizabeth store water during drought. Option 1, tank grants: cost J$30 million, benefits valued at J$45 million, 1,500 households helped. Option 2, low-interest loans for tanks: cost J$20 million, benefits J$26 million, 800 households helped. Option 3, an information campaign on water saving: cost J$6 million, benefits J$9 million, 600 households change habits. The grant would require households to pay J$15,000 towards each tank.

c3.title: Homework centres in Westmoreland
c3.text: Four years ago a ministry set up homework centres in 12 of the 30 primary schools in Westmoreland. Over four years the pass rate in the numeracy and literacy test at these 12 schools rose from 48% to 62%. At 12 similar schools with no centre, it rose from 48% to 55%. The programme costs J$24 million a year for 960 pupils. Most centres are in or near Savanna-la-Mar; none is in the remote hill communities. The funding comes from a donor grant that ends in two years.

c4.title: A policy paper for the board of a licensing agency
c4.text: Alicia Brown, a senior policy officer at a government licensing agency in Kingston, prepares a paper on a proposed new licence fee. The board meets on 14 June and papers must reach the board secretary 10 days before the meeting. A Green Paper on the proposal drew 400 written submissions, of which 120 opposed the fee. Her draft is 25 pages long and sets out three options with a recommendation.

c5.title: A proposed price-labelling rule for small shops
c5.text: A ministry proposes a rule that 1,800 small shops must label pre-packed goods with clear prices, setting aside about 5 hours a year to do so. An hour of a shopkeeper's time is valued at J$1,500. The ministry expects benefits to consumers of J$20 million a year. Another ministry's agency already requires price displays in a different format. The policy officer, Delroy Campbell, is asked to advise whether the rule should go ahead, and wonders whether the ministry has the power to impose it.

questions.q: Which item belongs in the roots of Marcia's problem tree, as a cause rather than an effect?
o: Vendors cannot pay at the one office during their trading hours
The corporation is short of money for the market repairs it has planned
Vendors who do pay on time feel that the system treats them unfairly
The Mandeville market slowly becomes dirty, crowded and run down
questions.why: Causes explain why the problem happens, and an office whose opening hours do not match the vendors' trading hours is one. The other options are effects that follow from unpaid fees.

questions.q: What percentage of the 150 stallholders surveyed said they did not know the date fees are due, and what does it suggest?
o: 60%, which suggests lack of information is a main cause worth acting on
40%, which suggests most vendors know the date and are choosing not to pay
90%, which suggests that every stallholder in the market is unaware of it
60%, which proves that all 400 stalls in the market are unaware of it
questions.why: 90 / 150 = 0.60, so 60%. It is a sample, so it suggests (not proves) a cause for the whole market, and it points to information as a cause.

questions.q: Which response is the most proportionate for the finance committee to consider first?
o: Text reminders and weekend payment points, then penalties for those who still do not pay
Closing the stall of every vendor in arrears until each one pays in full at once
A public notice at the market gate naming every vendor who owes fees to the corporation
A by-law that doubles the fee for all stallholders from the start of next month
questions.why: The causes are lack of information, inconvenient payment and no follow-up. Fix those first and enforce against those who still refuse. The other options punish before the causes are treated.

questions.q: Which is the best SMART policy objective for this problem?
o: Cut stall-fee arrears from J$18 million to below J$9 million by 31 March
Improve the way that market fees are collected from the stallholders at Mandeville
Make sure that all vendors fully understand their duty to pay the fees on time
Reduce arrears as quickly as the corporation is able to over the coming year
questions.why: It is specific, measurable (J$18 m to under J$9 m), has a baseline and target, and a date. The others have no number or deadline, so success could not be judged.

questions.q: Which option has the highest net benefit, and what is it?
o: Option 1, at J$15 million
Option 2, at J$6 million
Option 3, at J$3 million
Option 1, at J$45 million
questions.why: Net benefit is benefits minus costs. Option 1: 45 - 30 = 15; Option 2: 26 - 20 = 6; Option 3: 9 - 6 = 3. J$45 million is only Option 1's gross benefit.

questions.q: Which statement about the benefit-cost ratios is correct?
o: Options 1 and 3 both have a ratio of 1.5, so the ratio alone cannot separate them
Option 3 has the highest ratio because it is the option that costs the least money
Option 2 has a ratio of 1.3, which is below 1, so it would lose money for the ministry
Option 1 has a ratio of 1.5 while Option 3 has a ratio of 3.0 because it is cheaper
questions.why: 45 / 30 = 1.5 and 9 / 6 = 1.5; Option 2 is 26 / 20 = 1.3, which is still above 1 and so a gain. Because ratios tie, use net benefit and other criteria as well.

questions.q: Which option has the lowest cost per household helped, and what should the adviser say about it?
o: Option 3, at J$10,000 per household, but it helps the fewest households and has the smallest net benefit
Option 1, at J$20,000 per household, so it is the cheapest and needs no further checks before approval
Option 2, at J$25,000 per household, because loans let households spread the cost over time and so help more
Option 3, at J$6,000 per household, so it should be chosen because it costs the least overall
questions.why: Option 3 is 6,000,000 / 600 = J$10,000; Option 1 is J$20,000; Option 2 is J$25,000. Cost per household is one criterion; scale and net benefit matter as well.

questions.q: Which extra check should the adviser make before recommending the grants, given the J$15,000 payment required from each household?
o: Whether the poorest households could afford the payment and so be left out
Whether the ministry could print the grant application forms more cheaply
Whether households in Kingston would also like to receive a similar grant
Whether grants could be paid without keeping a record of each recipient
questions.why: Equity asks who gains and who loses. A co-payment can shut out the poorest households, who may need help most, so advise on support or exemptions for them.

questions.q: What is the best estimate of the effect of the homework centres on the pass rate?
o: 7 percentage points, the covered schools' rise minus the comparison schools' rise
14 percentage points, because that is the full rise seen at the covered schools
7%, because the comparison schools rose by 7 and that is the effect on the centres
62 percentage points, because that is the pass rate reached by the covered schools
questions.why: The comparison schools show what would probably have happened anyway (a rise of 7 points). The policy's own effect is 14 - 7 = 7 percentage points. The rise is in points, not percent.

questions.q: The cost for 960 pupils is J$24 million a year. Which figure and criterion does this give?
o: J$25,000 per pupil, a measure of efficiency
J$40,000 per pupil, a measure of equity
J$25,000 per pupil, a measure of relevance
J$2,400 per pupil, a measure of sustainability
questions.why: 24,000,000 / 960 = 25,000. Cost per person helped tests efficiency: could the same results be had at lower cost?

questions.q: That no centre serves the remote hill communities is a finding about which evaluation criterion?
o: Equity, because some groups are missing out on the benefit
Efficiency, because the cost per pupil there would be higher than elsewhere
Effectiveness, because the pass rate in those communities did not change
Relevance, because the problem of low pass rates no longer exists there
questions.why: Equity asks who benefits and who is missed. A policy can work well for those covered and still be unfair if some groups cannot reach it.

questions.q: The funding comes from a donor grant that ends in two years. What should the evaluator advise?
o: Treat it as a sustainability risk and recommend a plan for local funding or a cheaper model
Leave it alone, because the end of the grant is a matter for the donor, not the ministry
End the programme now, because it cannot be kept going without the donor's grant
Expand the centres to all 30 schools while the grant lasts, without any funding plan
questions.why: Sustainability asks whether results will last when support ends. Advise on how to keep what works, for example by absorbing costs in the budget or using a cheaper model.

questions.q: By what date must Alicia's paper reach the board secretary?
o: 4 June
24 May
14 June
7 June
questions.why: The board meets on 14 June and the paper is due 10 days before, so 14 - 10 = 4 June.

questions.q: What percentage of the Green Paper submissions opposed the fee, and how should the paper use the figure?
o: 30%, reported with the reasons given and the groups that opposed it
30%, so the other 70% of submissions can be counted as support for the fee
120%, which is the number of submissions that opposed the proposed fee
30%, which can be left out of the paper because consultation does not bind the board
questions.why: 120 / 400 = 30%. Consultation is not a vote: those who did not write have not necessarily agreed. Report the reasons and groups so decision-makers understand the concerns.

questions.q: What should Alicia put on the first page of her 25-page paper?
o: A short summary of the issue, her recommendation and the main reasons
A detailed history of the licensing agency since the day it was founded
The full list of all 400 submissions in the order in which they were received
The tables of calculations for each option, without any explanation of them
questions.why: Busy decision-makers read the first page. It should give the issue, the recommendation and the main reasons; detail and data go in annexes.

questions.q: At the meeting a board member asks, 'Which option do you prefer?' What should Alicia do?
o: Recommend one option and explain the reasons that come from her analysis
Say that choosing is the board's business and give the board no view at all
Recommend whichever option the chairperson seems most likely to favour
Offer to prepare a fourth option and ask the board to delay its decision
questions.why: An adviser's job is to give a reasoned recommendation. The board still decides, but it benefits from a clear view based on the evidence, not on what the chair prefers.

questions.q: What is the yearly compliance cost of the proposed price-labelling rule for the 1,800 shops?
Compared with benefits of J$20 million, what does the cost suggest, and what should the adviser add?
o: A net benefit of about J$6.5 million a year, with a note on assumptions and on small shops
A loss of J$6.5 million a year for the economy, so the rule should be rejected at once
A net benefit of J$20 million, since the shops and not the state pay the compliance cost
A net benefit of J$13.5 million a year, because that is the cost the shops will carry
questions.why: 20 - 13.5 = 6.5. The sum is favourable, but a good RIA states its assumptions and checks the burden on small firms.

questions.q: What must Delroy confirm before recommending the rule?
o: That the ministry has legal power to impose the requirement
That the largest supermarkets have asked the ministry for the rule
That the rule will be welcomed by the newspapers and radio
That the rule can be explained to shopkeepers in a single sentence
questions.why: A public body can only use powers its law gives it. A rule without legal authority could be challenged and fail.

questions.q: The other ministry's agency already requires price displays in a different format. What should Delroy advise?
o: Align the two requirements with the other ministry so that shops face one clear rule
Introduce the new format and leave shops to cope with two different requirements
Cancel the other agency's rule without first consulting that agency
Ignore the overlap, since the other agency's rule is not this ministry's concern
questions.why: Policy coherence means that policies work together. Conflicting rules add cost for shops and confusion; a joined-up approach is the sound advice.
